content: Clindamycin phosphate, when administered orally or parenterally, has been associated with severe colitis, which can potentially result in patient death. Even the topical formulation of clindamycin can lead to systemic absorption of the antibiotic through the skin. The use of both topical and systemic clindamycin has been reported to cause diarrhea, bloody diarrhea, and colitis, including pseudomembranous colitis. Research indicates that toxins produced by Clostridia bacteria are a primary cause of antibiotic-associated colitis. This condition is typically characterized by severe, persistent diarrhea, intense abdominal cramping, and may involve the passage of blood and mucus. Endoscopic examination may reveal pseudomembranous colitis. Diagnostic confirmation can be aided by stool cultures for Clostridium difficile and stool assays for C. difficile toxins. If significant diarrhea occurs, clindamycin should be discontinued immediately. In cases of severe diarrhea, large bowel endoscopy should be considered to establish a definitive diagnosis. The use of antiperistaltic agents, such as opiates or diphenoxylate with atropine, may prolong or worsen the condition and should be avoided. Vancomycin has been shown to be effective in treating antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis caused by Clostridium difficile. The typical adult dosage of vancomycin is 500 milligrams to 2 grams per day, administered orally in three to four divided doses over a course of 7 to 10 days. Cholestyramine or colestipol resins can bind vancomycin in vitro. If both a resin and vancomycin are to be administered concurrently, it is advisable to separate the timing of their administration to avoid interference. It is important to note that diarrhea, colitis, and pseudomembranous colitis have been observed to develop even several weeks after the cessation of oral or parenteral clindamycin therapy.
